A comprehensive matching of the Standard Model to an effective field theory at one-loop has been achieved, covering all possible dimension-6 operators up to a specific level of precision. This calculation, conducted within the framework of dimensional regularization, yields results that conform to the Ward identities and other key properties of the Standard Model. Notably, a novel approach to parameterize the vertices has been developed, enabling the direct derivation of the matching coefficients. This simplification has facilitated the identification of the physical parameters of the Standard Model within the effective field theory, including a demonstration that the $\rho$ parameter remains unchanged in the matching. This work provides a foundation for the application of matching in more complex scenarios, such as those involving non-renormalizable effective operators.

The field of machine learning has emerged as a distinct area of research within the broader field of computer science, drawing heavily from statistics, mathematics, and computer science. It has become a driving force behind the development of innovative products and services, revolutionizing the way we live and work. This report provides an overview of the core concepts in machine learning, including learning theory, neural networks, kernel methods, and deep learning, as well as its applications in natural language processing, computer vision, time series analysis, and network analysis. It also highlights the strategic initiatives and partnerships of leading tech companies, such as Google, Facebook, Microsoft, and IBM, in advancing machine learning and related technologies like artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things.

This paper presents a novel terminal sliding mode control strategy designed to minimize settling time by optimally switching control in the sub-space of fastening. A novel approach, the geodesic algorithm, is proposed to identify the optimal switching surface. By incorporating the reaching condition and the optimal switching surface, a new sliding mode surface is derived. A new sliding mode control is developed by combining the geodesic algorithm with the terminal sliding mode control, which is then evaluated through simulations to demonstrate its effectiveness.

The use of ultrasonic resonance techniques to analyze the internal structure of lithium-ion batteries has significant potential for quality control in industrial settings. This study explores the practical application of this method in real-world scenarios by examining the internal state of lithium-ion cells. The cells were subjected to various stress tests and their responses were then measured and analyzed using an ultrasonic resonance technique. The results showed that the internal structure of the cells underwent significant changes, which can be attributed to the redistribution of active materials, the deformation of anodes, and the elongation of cathode layers. The study's findings highlight the importance of accurately understanding the internal structure of lithium-ion cells to ensure safe and efficient operation during prolonged use.

This paper presents a novel approach to designing flatness-based controllers for a class of discrete-time systems. Building on existing knowledge of controller design in the continuous-time domain, it is clear that discrete-time systems require a different method of flatness inversion to effectively track desired trajectories. The key contribution of this work is the development of a unified framework that enables the creation of flatness-based controllers for both continuous-time and discrete-time systems. The paper also explores the relationship between traditional discrete-time models and lifting techniques, ultimately leading to a deeper understanding of flatness-based controller design in both contexts.

We've developed a method to fine-tune a pre-trained image description model using a curated dataset of around 20,000 images. This fine-tuning process involves generating descriptive captions based on the images and collecting user feedback to identify areas for improvement. In this work, we explore the idea that combining the strengths of the curated dataset lies in its smaller size and human feedback, and the pre-trained model's capabilities come from its large web-based dataset. We've demonstrated that by merging these two approaches, we can create a model that produces high-quality image descriptions. This hybrid model is then used to generate descriptive formats that are valuable for human feedback collection. The goal is to utilize human feedback to enhance the model's performance on specific image description tasks, such as describing fashion items.

We establish a tight bound on the maximum number of strings of a given size that can be chosen such that no two strings share a substring of a certain size $2k+1$ by considering these strings as edges on a graph. This bound is derived from a more general result that sets an upper limit on the number of strings based on the size of the most extensive well-connected subset of strings. This well-connected subset can consist of strings that share overlapping substrings.

We characterise one and two-sided restriction semigroups through their representation within ordered Ehresmann semigroups. Additionally, a description is given for restriction semigroups that can be arranged in a partial order while retaining congruence closure properties.

We investigate the optimal kernel width for a self-attention network with 1 trillion parameters using a Gaussian kernel, which is found to be approximately 1.1 by analyzing the decay of the attention head's weights.

BIO$_{3}$ nanoparticles were created using a hydrothermal method and examined for their optical and photocatalytic properties. The results showed that the nanoparticles have a bandgap of 2.1 eV, which is 0.2 eV lower than the bulk material, and this difference can be attributed to the nanoparticles' surface states. The nanoparticles demonstrated strong light absorption across the visible and near-infrared spectrum, and their photocatalytic performance was evaluated by measuring hydrogen production under UV and visible light. The most effective conditions for photocatalysis involved a 5% BiVO$_{4}$/BIO$_{3}$ core/shell structure under visible light with a power density of 0.5 W/g, and this resulted in the highest hydrogen production rate of 1.1 × 10$^{-6}$ mol/g per minute.

The $331$ model, a theoretical framework that goes beyond the Standard Model, is based on the concept of a non-Abelian $SU(3)$ group that includes a $U_1$ subgroup with two distinct charges. This model naturally explains the existence of three families of quarks and leptons by introducing mass-generating mechanisms for the bottom quark and tau lepton, which are achieved through a scalar field that interacts with a charged leptoquark and a charged scalar particle, respectively. The model predicts the existence of a scalar particle that can be produced through the decay of a heavy scalar boson, which is then detected via its interaction with a photon. The model also accounts for the observed anomalies in $b \to s \gamma$ transitions, and predicts that the decay of a heavy scalar particle will primarily produce a photon accompanied by a tau lepton.

We introduce a novel approach to inferring the 3D pose and shape of a grasped object using a single RGB camera. This method leverages a signed distance field (SDF) representation to capture the 3D object's shape and a low-dimensional latent space to model its pose. The SDF is learned using an implicit network, which is trained to reconstruct the object's surface from a given point cloud. The latent space is learned by mapping 6-DoF poses to latent codes and training a conditional generator network to reconstruct the SDF from these codes. The latent code for a given pose is obtained by projecting a 2D image of the object. Our method's key advantage is its ability to reconstruct the object's surface without relying on a specific template or 3D model, allowing it to generalize to novel shapes. The latent code also encodes the object's pose in a compact and meaningful way. Our results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing methods in shape and pose estimation on a variety of hand-held objects.

A novel approach, Equal Contrast, has been developed to efficiently analyze long time series of H$\alpha$ data obtained from ground-based telescopes, focusing on chromospheric variations. This method enables the identification of key factors influencing the chromosphere, such as magnetic fields, by employing a two-step process. Firstly, the most significant contributors to the chromospheric signal are pinpointed through a process of feature selection. Subsequently, the most relevant features are selected and combined in a second step to construct a compact model capable of accurately predicting chromospheric variations. This methodology has been successfully applied to a dataset of H$\alpha$ center-line images obtained from the GREGOR solar imager, resulting in a model that can predict chromospheric variations with a high degree of accuracy. This model has been validated by comparing its predictions with those of a widely used forward model, the MHD radiative magnetohydrodynamic model, for a specific active region.

The LHCb experiment has conducted a search for a novel type of particle, specifically the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay process, using data collected from proton-proton collisions at 7 and 8 TeV centre-of-mass energies, amounting to an integrated luminosity of 3 fb$^{-1}$. No substantial deviation from the standard model predictions was found for the product of branching fraction and form factor in the dimuon mass squared range from 0.05 to 1.7 GeV$^2$, resulting in an upper limit of the decay rate at  the 90\% confidence level, specifically 2.4(3.0) fb. This finding represents the most restrictive constraint on the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ branching fraction to date.

A key challenge in distributed symbolic execution is developing an efficient search strategy that balances thoroughness and speed. To address this issue, we've created a novel approach called test-depth partitioning, which empowers a leader to delegate the search strategy to individual workers. By dividing the test-depth range into manageable sections and assigning optimal segments to each worker, test-depth partitioning provides the flexibility to switch between aggressive and conservative strategies. The approach achieves this by analyzing each segment's test failure rate and adjusting the search strategy accordingly. The test-depth partitioning technique has been integrated into the KMP symbolic execution engine, yielding a 1.3 times performance improvement compared to a previously optimized, single-strategy engine.

The decay of magnetic remanence in an ensemble of randomly positioned and oriented anisotropic magnetic nanoparticles is studied under specific conditions.  A theoretical model accounting for the nanoparticles' anisotropy and random orientation is developed and applied to simulate various scenarios.  These simulations reveal that the magnetic decay rate depends on the angle between the magnetic field and the particles' anisotropy axis.  As a result, the magnetic decay is found to follow a specific exponential pattern that can be adjusted by varying the concentration of nanoparticles and their magnetic properties.  This theoretical framework is used to analyze the magnetic properties of a specific type of nanoparticle and the authors suggest its application in the design of magnetic data storage devices.

Federated learning enables training large models across numerous devices while keeping the models local, thus preserving user privacy. However, this approach faces a significant hurdle in the form of communication constraints, particularly in environments without a central server. To overcome this challenge, we propose an innovative method called Online Push-Sum (OPS), which empowers a group of devices to collaboratively learn models without relying on a central server. By utilizing OPS, devices can efficiently share their local models through a process of pushing and communication, ultimately achieving a unified global model. We demonstrate that OPS converges under a specific condition and validate its performance by comparing it to other methods on various datasets, showing comparable or superior results in the absence of communication limitations.

Predicting dialog acts is a crucial step in understanding the intent behind conversations. While current models have seen success in predicting acts from individual utterances, they still struggle to incorporate the broader context of a conversation. This study investigates how incorporating preceding short texts enhances dialog act prediction, specifically through the DIALACT dataset, which provides annotated short context for over 100,000 utterances. Our results show that predicting dialog acts from short contexts improves model performance, and combining this approach with other models can further boost accuracy. Additionally, our analysis reveals that predicting dialog acts under short context conditions can serve as a pre-training task to improve model performance on unseen data.

We've developed a telecentric etalon-based spectrometer that outperforms its collimated counterpart in terms of resolution and stability. The device's etalon is designed with a unique non-normalized surface to minimize optical aberrations, thereby enhancing resolution and reducing temperature sensitivity. Our instrument achieves an impressive wavelength accuracy of 10 cm-1 and demonstrates stability over 24 hours at a 1 K accuracy. Its high precision also allows for the detection of subtle changes in the Sun's spectral lines, which can indicate the instrument's temperature fluctuations. Our device's performance is showcased by analyzing the spectra of the Sun and a Lambda Aquarii star, highlighting its potential for precise radial velocity measurements. With its exceptional performance, this instrument sets a new standard for precision spectroscopy.

A set of points in the plane, marked with distinct integers, can be labeled in such a way that any two points with a certain distance relationship are adjacent only if their integers differ by a specific amount, a constant c. We prove that for any set of n points, there is a labeling where for any subset of k points, there are a sufficient number of other points, specifically a function of n, k, and c, whose labels ensure that they are connected to the subset only through a single edge. This resolves a problem of Erdos, Szemeredi, and Galvin and improves a result of Pach and Pivato.

The codelet execution model for program segments in codelets is proposed to be the core of a large-scale chiplet architecture, supporting billions of codelet instances. Codelets are defined as self-contained program segments that can be combined to form a program. The codelet execution model is built around a custom instruction set architecture (ISA) that enables efficient execution by a codelet core. The codelet core is paired with a codelet accelerator that performs tasks such as codelet communication, synchronization, and error handling. The codelet execution model is evaluated using a benchmark of 10 codelet programs and 100 codelet instances, demonstrating its potential to achieve high performance and energy efficiency by executing multiple codelet instances in parallel.

In survival analysis, a common task is to estimate a hazard function, which can be approached by breaking it down into its gradient and a Legendre basis. We propose a presmoothing technique that applies a smoothing spline to these components before using them to estimate the hazard function, which can be achieved by either a maximum likelihood method or a penalized likelihood approach. This presmoothing method has been found to improve the accuracy of estimators compared to traditional methods, such as maximum likelihood estimation. Furthermore, presmoothing can also be used to estimate the uncertainty of the hazard function by calculating the variance-covariance matrix of the estimators. We have developed a package in R that implements these methods, which can be applied to various types of data, including right-censored, interval-censored, and grouped data, and can handle different types of hazard functions, including those with a piecewise constant or linear function.

A specific metric dimension of a graph G is known as its NLD or nonlocal metric dimension, which is the smallest set of vertices that allows the identification of all pairs of vertices in G. In this study, we explore the NLDM (nonlocal diameter) of graphs and provide a characterization of graphs based on their diameter and metric dimension. We also find that graphs with a specific dimension of 1 or 2 are either complete graphs or graphs with a diameter of 2. Additionally, we find that non-regular graphs with a diameter of 2 and a specific dimension of 1 or 2 are either complete bipartite graphs or graphs with a specific structure. In the case of graphs with a diameter of 2 and a specific dimension of 1 or 2, we find that they are either complete bipartite graphs or graphs with a specific structure.

This paper introduces a universal side-channel attack strategy capable of targeting a broad range of side-channel resistant cryptosimulators under the side-channel model. The attack relies on analyzing power trace measurements and leverages a pre-trained classifier to identify side-channel signals within the power traces. The proposed method can adapt to various types of side-channel attacks and is effective against a wide variety of side-channel resistant architectures. Experimental results demonstrate the method's versatility in being applicable to multiple types of side-channel attacks and resistant architectures, as well as its ability to efficiently process large datasets.

By utilizing the relationship between the lower and upper limits of partial distances within a k-partite metric framework, we establish a method to reduce the size of polarization kernels. This reduction is achieved by determining the precise lower and upper limits of partial distances, which are essential for evaluating the tightness of polarization kernels. The derived bounds enable us to identify the exact minimum and maximum values of partial distances, thereby allowing us to derive the tightest possible polarization kernel constraints.

A novel approach to self-supervised denoising of seismic data is presented, 
where the initial supervised training stage utilizes a synthetic dataset, 
after which the model transitions to self-supervised denoising. 
This initial stage refines the model's ability to capture subtle seismic 
characteristics, such as subtle faults within the data, which are imperceptible 
to the human eye. The self-supervised stage then refines the model's ability to 
detect noise patterns, such as multiple sources of interference, 
enabling the model to learn to remove these noise patterns from the data. 
This approach is evaluated using a publicly available dataset, 
showcasing the model's effectiveness in removing various types of noise sources.

The influence of real photon emission on the cross-section asymmetry is investigated in lepton-proton scattering processes, specifically the scattering of longitudinally polarized neutrinos by unpolarized protons. The study focuses on neutrino-proton scattering at low energy and calculates the resulting cross-section asymmetry for muon and tau neutrinos, examining both the inelastic and total channels.

Theoretical research on the electronic structure of Mott insulators containing doped holes has been conducted, with a focus on the impact of spin-polaronic ladders. Our findings indicate that the electronic structure is characterized by a self-consistent interaction between holes and spin waves, leading to a non-linear relationship between holes and spin polaritons. This non-linear relationship gives rise to a non-linear interaction between holes, which in turn leads to a phase separation into spin-polarized regions. Consequently, holes are localized in these regions, where they exhibit a non-linear relationship with spin polaritons. This localized hole distribution results in a non-linear spin wave spectrum, which in turn affects the electronic structure of the system. Our research suggests that the electronic structure of Mött insulators containing doped holes can be reorganized by controlling the hole concentration and spin wave intensity.

This study introduces a novel estimation method for continuous treatments that maintains robustness with regards to key assumptions commonly used in causal analysis. The proposed estimator is derived from a weighted combination of the average treatment effect and the control group outcome, with the weight being the proportion of units with treatment outcomes below the control group's average. The estimator is specifically defined when the average treatment effect is zero, in which case it takes the value of the control group's average. The method is grounded in a flexible regression model that accommodates nonlinearity and heteroskedasticity, and its finite-sample performance is evaluated through simulation studies. The estimator is further demonstrated in a real-world application involving the estimation of a continuous treatment effect on the difference in mean outcomes.

Recent research on starshades has gained momentum, leading to a surge in the number of scientists exploring this area. This surge presents an opportunity for the scientific community to reap benefits from collaborative efforts. To illustrate this point, we examine how recent research on starshades can be integrated with ongoing studies focused on exoplanets and star formation. We also discuss potential collaborations with areas of recent research on star-planet interactions and star mass loss. Furthermore, we highlight areas where further research on starshades may lead to new breakthroughs. By exploring these connections, we aim to demonstrate the value of cross-disciplinary research efforts and their potential to drive significant advancements in our understanding of starshades.

Suicide prevention efforts are hindered by the rapid spread of suicidal information online. To address this issue, we have developed the Robin dataset, a collection of suicidal texts from Twitter that goes beyond existing public datasets by including more nuanced suicidal texts. This dataset contains 1,761 labeled texts, which we plan to utilize in future research. Our dataset is now available for use at https://github.com/robin-suicide-ai/robin-dataset.
A supersymmetric action is formulated for the super-Schwarzian from the constraints of a single fermionic variable in a supersymmetric theory.

The presented research has implications for both continuous and discrete dynamical systems within a rational framework, with specific applications in the fields of dynamical, difference, partial, and integral equations.

This study focuses on a class of electrically charged, anti-de Sitter black holes within the framework of four-dimensional General Relativity, specifically with a non-linear electrodynamic model that incorporates a specific Lagrangian $L(Q) = f(Q) = Q^2$, where $Q$ represents a charge density. The investigation delves into thermodynamic properties of these black holes, including their critical behavior and thermodynamic phase equilibrium.

We consider a linear form with integral coefficients, expressed as $f(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = a_1x_1 + \ldots + a_nx_n$. Our analysis focuses on the existence of infinite Sidon sets, i.e., sets of integers with no non-trivial linear combinations that equal $0$. We prove that if the system of equations $f(x) = 0$ has a small rank, we can find an infinite Sidon set for $f$. This is achieved by constructing a system of equations $f(x) = 0$ with a small rank, then using a theorem of van der Waerden to find an infinite Sidon set.

We explore the quantum dynamics of a spin-1/2 chain in contact with a low-temperature spin bath, and examine the system's behavior as it undergoes a quantum phase transition. Through the use of a semigroup approach, we demonstrate that susceptibility to the external magnetic field is connected to the geometric phase, and that this relationship remains robust even in the presence of system-bath interactions. Furthermore, we analyze the relationship between the geometric phase and critical exponents, and investigate the impact of dephasing interactions on the system's critical properties.

The relaxation of ferromagnetic systems is studied in high-temperature scenarios, where critical fluctuations significantly impact the cooling process.  A mean-field model incorporating the critical exponent $\beta$ and the cooling rate $\Gamma$ is utilized to determine the system's final equilibrium state.  By employing the finite-size scaling theory, the system's behavior is analyzed and found to be influenced by the cooling rate.  A key outcome of this study is the existence of a finite cooling rate that prevents the system from achieving its equilibrium state.  Furthermore, the system's behavior is characterized by a power-law relaxation below a certain temperature, which depends on the cooling rate.  A notable characteristic of this power-law relaxation is the presence of a characteristic exponent that depends on the cooling rate.  A comparison of the system's behavior with experimental data reveals that the critical exponents $\beta$ and the characteristic exponents exhibit a dependence on the cooling rate. The transition from localization to ordering in quasicrystals is facilitated by quasiperiodicity, and studying the localization of states in quasicrystals can reveal the underlying dynamics of this transition.  In this research, we investigate the critical properties of a two-dimensional quasiperiodic Kronig-Penney model, specifically the bound states, by employing a method that maps the two-dimensional model to a network of interconnected loops.  By analyzing the eigenstates of this network, we can gain insights into the bound states of the original model, and our results indicate that the critical properties are closely tied to the existence of flat eigenstates in the network, specifically those that are invariant under certain unitary transformations.  These invariant states correspond to states that are localized at specific sites in the original quasiperiodic model, and our research reveals that the existence of these states is a key factor in understanding the localization of bound states in quasicrystals.

To create effective task-oriented dialogue systems across multiple languages, we must develop a method for training these systems using limited, high-quality, and culturally sensitive data. Currently, systems are trained using English dialogue scripts, which are then matched with generic responses in other languages through machine translation. This approach often yields subpar results, as it fails to account for cultural nuances and leads to generic, irrelevant responses. In this research, we explore the possibility of using large-scale, unsupervised machine translation models to improve cross-lingual dialogue systems. We examine the performance of these models, both alone and in conjunction with limited, high-quality human-annotated data, and compare it to the standard method of matching pre-annotated English scripts with machine-translated responses. The results demonstrate that our approach produces superior results, surpassing the existing standard in multiple languages.

The RNA-seq time series analysis enables the examination of differential expression and splicing by comparing multiple conditions through the integration of statistical and machine learning methods. A popular approach involves the use of empirical Bayes methods, which leverage shrinkage to estimate gene-wise variance. A novel algorithm, DESeq2, has been widely adopted for RNA-seq data analysis due to its efficiency and effectiveness. A new algorithm, rseq, builds upon DESeq2's variance shrinkage while optimizing multiple testing correction and the estimation of variance for each gene. A comprehensive comparison of DESeq2 and rseq was conducted using simulated and real RNA-seq data, revealing that rseq outperforms DESeq2 in terms of accuracy and robustness.

The growing need for technical measures to safeguard personal data in the digital realm has given rise to a new profession: data protection officers. These officers are tasked with ensuring that an organization's technical data handling methods align with its declared data protection policies. However, there's a notable gap between these legal requirements and the actual technology implementation, which often involves costly reimplementation of security measures. To bridge this gap, we propose an interactive workflow that enables effective collaboration between legal and engineering teams throughout the entire implementation process. Our approach is designed to be adaptable to various data protection policies and security measures, and is underpinned by a comprehensive framework that we detail in this research.

We utilize the Color Glass Condensate formalism to investigate correlations in proton-proton collisions at non-linear levels. Within this framework, initial conditions are simulated using the GLS model for azimuthal correlations in three-particle events. Our calculations demonstrate that non-linear effects significantly impact correlations, exceeding linear regime predictions and closely aligning with experimental data in cumulant and factorial measurements.

The production of light nuclei such as deuterons, helium isotopes, and tritons in high-energy collisions is studied using a dynamical model that incorporates both string breaking and coalescence sources. These coalescence sources are modeled as having a finite size and lifetime, allowing for a detailed examination of their impact on the production of light nuclei. The results show that the finite lifetime of coalescence sources can significantly affect the production yield and shape of light nucleus spectra, and that this effect can be tested in future experiments at RHIC and LHC. The production of light nuclei is found to be sensitive to the minimum kinetic fraction required for particle coalescence, and that this sensitivity can be used to constrain this parameter. The production of light nuclei is also found to be affected by the presence of a hard core in coalescence sources, and that this effect can be used to study the production of light nuclei in high-energy collisions.

The discovery of numerous rocky exoplanets has led to a greater understanding of their atmospheric compositions, with implications for their potential habitability. However, the vast array of atmospheric compositions observed so far, including those on planets like Kepler-36b and WASP-12b, differ significantly from those found on Earth. To address this discrepancy, we have developed a new model that simulates the atmospheric evolution of rocky exoplanets, taking into account the effects of atmospheric loss and the incorporation of various core compositions. By analyzing the model's results, we have identified key factors that influence the diversity of atmospheric compositions, including core composition, atmospheric loss, and the presence of volatile elements. We have also investigated the potential for life to exist on exoplanets, and our findings suggest that the conditions necessary for life to thrive are unlikely to be met on planets with high atmospheric losses, regardless of their core composition.

We've developed a comprehensive formula for calculating the number of distinct colors that can be applied to the vertices of a circulant graph, provided its jump lengths are three or less. Additionally, we've identified specific patterns for specific types of these graphs, including those with jump lengths of one, two or three. These findings also enable us to determine the exact minimum and maximum number of colors required for coloring these graphs, based on their structure. Specifically, we've discovered that all such graphs are colorable, except in a few exceptional cases. These exceptional cases include specific types of circulant graphs, such as the circulant graphs with jump lengths of two and three for certain graph sizes, as well as the circulant graphs with jump lengths of one, two and three for certain graph sizes.

This paper investigates the Nested Neumann algorithm within the context of regularized inverse problems, demonstrating its equivalence to a two-stage process using the Kaczmarz method. The algorithm's convergence rate is shown to be influenced by the depth of signal features within the solution space, quantified by the Inception depth. The study also provides theoretical explanations for the algorithm's effectiveness in low-noise scenarios and its slow convergence rate in noise-prone cases. Additionally, the researchers propose an improved variant of the algorithm, which incorporates a dynamic step size and convergence rate adjustment mechanism. The theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments.

The influence of cosmic friction on the enhancement of curvature perturbations during inflation is examined. The friction term significantly boosts curvature perturbations when the cosmic friction is positive, particularly in single-field inflation models, by increasing the sound speed. Conversely, in multi-field inflation models, the boost effect is dependent on the interplay between the sound speed and transfer function of curvature perturbations. A positive cosmic friction leads to a rise in the amplitude of curvature perturbations during inflation, causing the power spectrum to deviate from the standard scale-invariant form, particularly at small scales. Consequently, this amplification may yield large curvature perturbations during inflation, potentially triggering the end of inflation and giving rise to primordial black holes.

This research investigates how airlines utilize revenue management to influence demand, increase sales, and manage competition directly through fare offerings. The study develops a new method to calculate the revenue- enhancing effect of limited fares on airlines, and through experiments, it demonstrates the significance of this effect in the air transport market. The analysis also explores the relationship between demand, limited fares, and cannibalization, showing that offering lower fares can attract new customers but ultimately reduces sales of higher fares offered by the same airline.

The Casebase R package is an innovative tool designed to facilitate the creation of casebase models, offering a user-friendly interface to analyze survival data through a unique approach. By incorporating a new estimation method, the package enhances the capabilities of existing R functions, notably coxlm, to provide more accurate and reliable results, particularly in scenarios where the standard method may yield aberrant outcomes. Furthermore, the package's functionality has been successfully utilized in a real-world setting, where it effectively addressed a data anomaly that would have otherwise compromised the interpretability of the results, ultimately providing a more accurate and comprehensive understanding of the casebase model.

A novel semi-numeric method has been developed to solve particle physics problems that are typically represented by differential equations. This new method employs an iterative approach to solve these equations, which can be easily modified to incorporate various theoretical corrections in a straightforward manner. Notably, the method offers better accuracy compared to other techniques, such as the self-consistent solution, while also enabling the efficient integration of additional physics components in a flexible and efficient manner.

The conventional methods used in distributed file systems, such as POSIX, are inadequate in meeting the demands of modern cloud-based systems, particularly those built on object storage. This paper presents an innovative approach to integrate object storage capabilities into file systems, leveraging the existing infrastructure of distributed object storage systems like HDFS. The proposed system, known as HDFSFS, capitalizes on the scalability and reliability of object storage while delivering a high-performance, distributed file system. Through rigorous evaluation, it was demonstrated that HDFSFS surpasses HDFS in file metadata operations, file system image benchmarks, and Hadoop job execution performance.

In this research, we examine the most effective methods for allocating limited EV charging resources at parking lots with electrical connections. A central authority oversees the operation of these parking facilities, which are owned by private companies. These companies seek to maximize their profits, while the central authority aims to ensure fair resource distribution and efficient charging. We present a dynamic pricing system that addresses the central authority's concerns and is compatible with the parking companies' goals. This method ensures that EVs are charged efficiently and minimizes the negative impact on the companies' profit. A numerical study demonstrates the central authority's ability to control the charging distribution and the parking companies' ability to achieve high profits.

This paper proposes novel methods for generating Hermitian low-density parity-check codes with explicit structure, specifically Hermitian LCD codes and Hermitian linear complementary-dual codes. By utilizing these methods, it is possible to create new codes with explicit structure that have a significantly lower rate compared to the original codes they are derived from. The proposed construction also allows for the creation of Hermitian quasi-twisted LCD codes and Hermitian linear complementary-dual quasi-twisted codes.

In a study of black hole scattering in the context of Einstein gravity combined with a massless scalar field, the fifth-order scattering coefficients were calculated. This analysis was conducted for both low-energy and high-energy scenarios, where the latter was achieved by considering the effects of virtual black holes with masses comparable to their diameter. This research marks the first instance where such advanced calculations have been performed within a theory involving scalar fields. This analysis was made possible by employing a novel method of simplifying the metric to a form known as the "near-horizon" metric, which significantly reduced the complexity of the problem. This approach also facilitated the use of a straightforward method for evaluating the integrals that arise during the calculation process.

The rapid expansion of renewable energy systems is necessary to achieve clean electricity goals, but the increasing land requirements for solar and wind sites are causing significant issues. To address these challenges, we have developed a model that optimizes the development of solar and wind sites by minimizing the risk of land use conflicts through site selection. Our model considers the uncertainty associated with site risk and evaluates the impact of conflict minimization on the affordability of clean energy goals. Our results indicate that prioritizing conflict-free site selection for solar and wind sites increases the cost of achieving clean electricity goals by 4-12% and that optimizing site allocation based on risk levels can reduce conflicts by 50-60%.

Cluster-randomized trials frequently employ marginal analysis to assess the direct impact of a treatment, which involves comparing outcomes between treatment and control groups at the individual level. However, this approach is often based on assumptions that are not met in actual trials, resulting in biased estimates. A notable example of this is cluster-randomized flu vaccine trials, which have consistently found no significant evidence of individual-level protection offered by the vaccine. This paper argues that the estimated effects in such cases are actually measuring a different impact, specifically the indirect effect that arises when a treatment reduces the transmission of a disease, ultimately leading to fewer individuals being exposed to the disease and experiencing its effects, even if they are not directly protected. The paper proposes a new method for estimating the direct impact of vaccination that takes into account this indirect effect, which has been shown to significantly increase the estimated effect size in flu vaccine trials, from 8% to 21%, and even higher in some cases.

This paper explores the topological properties of specific graph characteristics, focusing on the multiplicative degree-Kirchhoff index and the multiplicative degree-Zernov index. Various formulas are derived for these indices in terms of positive integer powers and their connections to other topological parameters are investigated. Additionally, the asymptotic behaviors of these graph characteristics, particularly as the graph size grows exponentially, are examined and their relationships to other topological network parameters are established.

We investigate contextual linear bandits under the assumption that the data is being transmitted over a channel with limited capacity. Our goal is to minimize the overall communication overhead, which is defined as the product of the number of communication rounds and the number of bits transmitted in each round. To achieve this, we propose an algorithm called CLiBAC. This algorithm leverages the context distribution to gain insight into the underlying parameter space and adjusts its communication strategy accordingly. Specifically, if the context distribution contains sufficient information about the parameter space, CLiBAC can reduce its communication overhead by requiring fewer bits per round. Our results demonstrate that CLiBAC can achieve near-optimal regret in terms of communication rounds while using only polylogarithmic bits per round. Furthermore, we show that no algorithm can do better than this in general.

To counteract the negative impact of class imbalance on predictive models, we employ oversampling, which involves duplicating minority instances. Nevertheless, oversampling can lead to overfitting, particularly when generating new instances from minority class data. Our proposed approach, oversampling resistance via random undersampling (RU), addresses this challenge by mitigating overfitting to oversampled data. This method works by randomly removing instances from the training set before model fitting, thereby ensuring that the model is not overly reliant on the artificially generated minority instances. Our approach is validated through experiments on various imbalanced binary classification datasets, which demonstrate that RU outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve.

The LHCb experiment has obtained precise measurements of certain particle decays. This research involves a detailed analysis of these decays, utilizing the results to enhance future measurements of the $C\!P$ angle $\gamma$ and future analyses on charm mixing and $C\!P$ violations. The study also examines the feasibility of constructing a partial amplitude model for specific decays and evaluates its effectiveness in determining key parameters.

A significant amount of research relies on reproducing previous results to validate findings, but there's a lack of understanding about how to effectively do so. To address this, we analyzed a dataset of 1.3 million papers to identify key predictors of research reproducibility. Our research revealed that certain metrics, such as citation rates and author rankings, can significantly contribute to the reproducibility of studies across multiple fields. Additionally, we found that combining these metrics can improve their contribution, and we've developed a new method for estimating the contribution of individual studies. Our results provide valuable insights for authors, reviewers, editors, and policy-makers, ultimately enhancing the quality and reproducibility of research.

A novel approach called "flying focus X" has been developed to rapidly steer a laser focus, offering a wide range of motion control options. By precisely directing the focus of a laser beam, this technique enables the precise manipulation of particles at the nanoscale. The method's versatility stems from its ability to seamlessly integrate with a wide variety of motion control systems, including optical, acoustic, and mechanical systems. The resulting focus can be steered at velocities exceeding 10 m/s, achieving high precision along the way, making it an ideal solution for applications like high-speed particle manipulation, rapid focusing of large areas, and fast laser scanning. The technique's flexibility and adaptability make it an attractive solution for a wide range of applications.

The FIRA HuroCup league has been driving advancements in humanoid robotics for over a decade, pushing the boundaries of what these robots can do. Composed of 20 teams from around the world, the HuroCup competitions have consistently showcased the progress and innovation in humanoid robotics, with a recent focus on the HUST Open, a new competition model, introduced in 2020. This paper will explore the HuroCup's past achievements and the challenges it has overcome, as well as the HUST Open's inception, its design, and early results, with a view to the HuroCup's future plans and the HuroCup league's continued growth and development.

In cross-domain recommendation, a central challenge arises from the disparity in source and target domains' feature distributions. To address this issue, we propose a novel solution that integrates metric learning into a transformer-based cross-domain recommendation framework. This approach enables the transformation of source domain features into the target domain's structural and semantic structure, effectively bridging the gap between domains. Through a series of experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, we demonstrate the efficacy of our method in achieving superior results compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

A novel automaton model, called the extended finite-state machine, has been proposed. In this framework, a finite-state machine interacts with its environment through a combination of input and output channels. The main contribution of this paper is to establish a comprehensive characterization of the expressive power of this model. The paper demonstrates that the expressiveness of this model heavily relies on the nature of the interactions between the machine and its environment. The paper provides explicit examples to illustrate this observation. Specifically, it is shown that an interaction model that involves only single-channel communication is less expressive than the interaction model that involves a combination of both input and output channels. The paper also shows that the expressiveness of this model is heavily influenced by the communication method used. For instance, it is shown that an interaction model that involves a pushdown store is less expressive than the interaction model that does not involve a pushdown store. The paper also provides a characterization of the expressiveness of this model in terms of the well-known pushdown automaton model.

A model for heat exchange in 2D plasma films has been developed, accounting for the complex interplay of plasma elements such as their density, temperature, and arrangement. This model incorporates the effects of plasma oscillations, interparticle collisions, and variations in particle size and speed. It also considers the impact of long-range electrostatic interactions and takes into account both the potential energy of plasma components and the forces they exert on one another. By applying the Boltzmann distribution, the model enables the calculation of energy exchange between plasma components and the resulting temperature variations within the film.

This study explores the relationship between counter machines and monadic second-order logic through the lens of trace semantics, while also considering the implications of two types of data constraints - equality and inequality - on this relationship. Our analysis reveals that a subset of counter machines, defined by their equality-based semantics, is equivalent in expressiveness to Coloured Petri nets. Furthermore, we discovered that a larger class of counter machines, defined by their inequality-based semantics, is expressively more powerful than all trace-equivalent systems, including those with equality-based constraints. Our findings also provide a clear characterisation of the most powerful monadic second-order logic with data, particularly when considering the inequality-based semantics.

To enhance the quality of synthesized high frame rate video from coronary angiography, researchers investigated the application of a video generation method using a generative adversarial network (GAN). This method leverages a large amount of low frame rate video data, eliminating the need for high volume labeled data. Experiments were conducted to evaluate the performance of the synthesis approach, which achieved a 20.53 dB peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and a 0.03 Frobenius distance (F-score) relative to the reference video when using a 60fps video. These results demonstrated a notable improvement over the baseline, which had a 16.12 dB PSNR and a 0.08 F-score. Additionally, the incorporation of a residual block in the generative model contributed to the enhancement of the synthesis quality.

The exceptionally low-background environment at FCC-ee will enable researchers to study the rare processes of heavy particles, such as top and beauty quarks, with greater sensitivity. This is particularly significant for investigating the source of CP-violation in the Standard Model, a topic that is crucial for resolving the weak charge puzzle. By leveraging the high luminosity of 5 ab^-1 at FCC-ee, scientists can conduct precise measurements of the branching ratios of rare decays, such as top quark decay into a tau lepton and beauty quark decay into an electron or muon, along with other rare particle decays. These studies will be complemented by searches for lepton flavor universality violations and anomalies in beauty quark decays, as well as the investigation of long-lived, exotic particles that could potentially explain the observed anomalies in the muon anomalous magnetic moment and antineutrino mass.

The recent experimental validation of CE$
u$NS has opened up a new area in dark matter searches, leveraging the same enhancement factor derived from neutrino interactions. We investigate the feasibility of using CE$
u$NS to detect dark matter in experiments, specifically those searching for WIMPs. We find that enhancements in neutrino interactions translate to substantial improvements in DM direct detection sensitivity, rivaling limits set by the LZ experiment. Moreover, combining LZ sensitivity with the CE$
u$NS enhancement factor yields competitive sensitivity with the Xenonn1T experiment.

We have developed a new method to calculate the gravitational influence of an intermediate-mass companion star on stars in the vicinity of a supermassive black hole, which is crucial for understanding the behavior of stars in the vicinity of active galactic nuclei. Our approach involves computing the gravitational perturbation of the companion star at various points in its orbit around the supermassive black hole, and then determining the resulting star orbits using a numerical method that takes into account the star's proximity to the black hole. This method allows us to calculate the star orbits for different configurations of the system and to compare the results with previous analytical models. Our approach can be applied to a range of scenarios, including the motion of the companion star, and can be used to predict the behavior of stars in the vicinity of active galactic nuclei. Our results show that the gravitational influence of the companion star can have a significant impact on the orbits of stars in the vicinity of the black hole, and can even lead to the formation of a stable, eccentric orbit around the black hole.

This research examines stochastic differential equations (SDEs) that are significantly impacted by fractional Brownian motion (FBM). The primary objective is to investigate how the value of the Hurst parameter $H$ affects the strong solution of such SDEs. The study begins by establishing a fundamental theorem stating that for any given Hurst parameter $H$ in the interval $(0,1)$, there exists a corresponding SDE with a lower $H$ and an additional drift component, both of which are defined by a sequence of measurable functions. The research further explores the scenario where the strong solution of the lower $H$ SDE is also a strong solution of the higher $H$ SDE, and it is proven that this relationship holds true for a subset of commonly used models, including the geometric Brownian motion. The study also investigates the scenario where the strong solution of the lower $H$ SDE is not a strong solution of the higher $H$ SDE, and it is shown that this discrepancy is a direct result of the non-uniqueness of the strong solution of the higher $H$ SDE. The study also examines the scenario where the strong solution of the lower $H$ SDE is not a strong solution of the lower $H$ SDE, and it is shown that this discrepancy is a direct result of the non-uniqueness of the strong solution of the lower $H$ SDE.

We investigate the application of the Cohen forcing method in constructing generic models for nonstationary ideals. Specifically, we demonstrate that it's feasible to create a nonstationary ideal λ with a Σ1 formula parameter and a unique generic model for every element in it. Furthermore, we show that if the nonstationary ideal NP is not unique, then there exists an element λ in NP such that no other nonstationary ideal π λ includes λ in its domain.

Multitask training in machine learning has been shown to significantly enhance task performance, yet the effectiveness of this approach remains largely unexplored due to the labor-intensive process of designing and conducting experiments. To address this limitation, we introduce MLWorkbench, an innovative platform that streamlines multitask training by offering a user-friendly, automated environment. With MLWorkbench, researchers can efficiently test various hypotheses related to multitask training, eliminating the need for extensive code modifications and resource-intensive computations. To demonstrate the capabilities of our platform, we present a series of experiments that validate its design and provide valuable insights into the benefits of multitask training.

The development of large-scale traffic sign datasets has significantly accelerated the advancement of deep learning-based object detection algorithms. This research paper presents OpenSigns, a massive traffic sign dataset comprising 1.5 million images, and explores the effectiveness of transfer learning using this dataset. OpenSigns surpasses existing datasets in scale and diversity, featuring 38 distinct sign categories, 19 different languages, and 19 distinct regions. This paper examines the impact of the number of training samples per class on traffic sign detection performance, and demonstrates that using OpenSigns leads to improved results, outperforming the popular MESSD dataset. Furthermore, OpenSigns showcases robustness in handling diverse scenarios, such as varying lighting conditions, and outperforms the state-of-the-art models when applied to challenging benchmarks. OpenSigns is made available under a permissive license, facilitating further research and development in the field.

Recommending items that users will find appealing is a complex task.  Traditional methods of recommending items rely on explicit feedback from users, which can be time-consuming and impractical.  To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed a new framework called SelfCF that utilizes implicit feedback from users to make accurate recommendations.  By employing a self-supervised learning approach, SelfCF enables the simultaneous training of its encoder and prediction head, which has led to a significant reduction in training time.  Furthermore, SelfCF's unique encoder architecture allows it to capture the relationships between items and their users more effectively, which has resulted in a significant improvement in recommendation accuracy.  Experimental results have demonstrated the effectiveness of SelfCF on multiple real-world datasets, with a notable improvement of up to 14.1% over existing state-of-the-art methods.

In this research, we're examining how to count smooth maps from a set of n-dimensional spaces to it, specifically under the constraint of additional complex conditions related to how these maps behave at particular points. We show that when considering these extra conditions, the problem can often be solved using a method called localization, which reduces it to a simpler case that doesn't involve the extra conditions. We also develop a more general approach to solving this problem by using a technique called motivic integration, which allows us to solve it in situations where the localization method doesn't work. Additionally, we use this more general approach to solve it in situations where the set of n-dimensional spaces is a particular type of space called a torus.

A theoretical study of the electronic and optical properties of a gapped Dirac semimetal has been conducted using a two-dimensional model, which was solved using the Green's function method. The results show that the density of states and optical conductivity exhibit a universal power-law behavior at high energies, and the obtained results are consistent with those of a gapped Dirac model in one dimension. The findings were further validated by comparing them with the numerical results of a lattice model, and the study also discusses the application of its results to the materials WTe$_2$ and Cd$_3$As$_2$.

We analyze a class of ordinary differential equations modeling population dynamics with periodic coefficients, where a small parameter influences the rate of change. This parameter, denoted $\varepsilon$, tends to zero, leading to distinct equilibrium behaviors based on the period of the coefficients' oscillations. For periods of two, we demonstrate that the rapid dynamics converge to a reduced, two-dimensional model, characterized by a slow dynamics component. For periods of three or greater, we show that the limiting behavior is governed by a single-dimensional model, with the slow dynamics component dominating. This research extends existing work on three-dimensional systems with decaying coefficients, offering a general framework applicable to coefficients with arbitrary periods.

Future gravitational wave detectors will be able to identify binary black hole mergers through multipoles beyond those of the second order. This study examines the potential for detecting binary black hole mergers in third-generation detectors, focusing on the (3,3) and (4,4) modes. It assesses the detectability of these modes in various sky locations, masses, and orbital orientations. The study also calculates the signal-to-noise ratios for detecting these modes in individual and combined detectors, including their ability to distinguish between different binary black hole populations. The results indicate that (3,3) and (4,4) modes will be detectable in third-generation detectors, with a higher signal-to-noise ratio for low-mass binaries. The (4,4) mode will be detectable in approximately 20% of binary black hole mergers, with a higher detectability in low-mass binaries. The study also shows that third-generation detectors will be able to identify approximately 40% of binary black hole mergers in a specific mass range, allowing for the determination of their orientations. The results also indicate that third-generation detectors will be able to identify approximately 20% of binary black hole mergers in a specific mass range, allowing for the determination of their orientations.
